answer:
Yes. The edge state survived on the real quantum computer.

What I ran: I built two 8-site SSH chains, with one qubit per site. The chain sits on garnet qubits QB20, QB19, QB18, QB14, QB13, QB8, QB3, QB4, in that order. I chose this line because it had the best two-qubit gate and readout quality in the current calibration. The end site is QB20. Each circuit starts with one electron on QB20 (that qubit set to 1). It then evolves to time 2 under H = sum of b (XX + YY) / 2, using 3 Trotter steps of 0.5 each. That comes to 42 CZ gates per circuit. One chain starts with a weak bond (0.3, 1.0, 0.3, ...). The other starts with a strong bond (1.0, 0.3, 1.0, ...). First I ran both circuits on garnet:mock as a test (job 01a160ac-aa24-72af-8f00-b52429bf5610, no credits). Then I ran the same two circuits as one real job on garnet with 1000 shots (job 01a160ac-eeb2-71d6-83d0-62df5bf59e8d). The API reports 1.0 billed second for the real job. No submit call raised an error.

What the numbers show:
- Weak-bond-first chain: a perfect machine running this circuit would find the electron on the end site 75.9% of the time. The real QPU found it there 73.1% of the time.
- Strong-bond-first chain: a perfect machine would give 14.5%. The real QPU gave 16.4%.
- About 71% of shots had exactly one 1, which is what a perfect machine gives every time. The other shots picked up errors from noise. Among the clean shots, the edge probability was 72.6% for the weak-bond-first chain and 14.0% for the strong-bond-first chain. Both are close to the ideal values.
- In the strong-bond-first chain, the most common result put the electron on the second site (451 of 1000 shots). That fits the strong first bond pulling it off the end.

The principle: in the SSH model, the type of bond at the end decides what happens. When the chain ends on a weak bond, a state forms that stays stuck to the end site. An electron placed there mostly stays put. When the chain ends on a strong bond, no such state exists, and the electron moves into the chain. The 73% versus 16% gap is large, even after 42 noisy two-qubit gates. Noise blurred the result only a little.

What this says about the real material: polyacetylene has the same alternating pattern of strong and weak bonds. The model predicts that a chain end or a defect where the pattern flips can hold a localized electron state. These states are the solitons that explain part of polyacetylene's conducting behavior. This experiment shows the effect in a small 8-site toy model on qubits. It does not simulate the real molecule. Real polyacetylene also has electron-electron forces, lattice vibrations, and long disordered chains. This model leaves all of those out.

Note on counts: these are Qiskit bitstrings. The rightmost character is site 0 (QB20), and the leftmost is site 7 (QB4). "counts" holds the weak-bond-first circuit. "counts_list" holds both circuits in order: weak-bond-first, then strong-bond-first. I took the ideal values from a noise-free simulation of the circuits the server received, which I read back from the job payload. The Trotter steps put these 0.4 to 0.8 points away from the exact model values of 76.7% and 14.2%.
